hardening.unit: release.yml (tag push, workflow_dispatch; build, rebuilds, same-bytes, judge legs, gather,
hardening.note: Release authorization rests on one identity: both rulesets give the admin role bypass_mode 'always', the only collaborator is that admin, and the release, pypi and github-pages environments have a branch/tag policy but no required reviewer. The tag-on-main check (release.yml:140) lives in the tagged commit's own workflow file, so it binds only an unmodified release.yml. Any process holding the owner's token (local automation included) can create a v* tag on a non-main commit with an edited release.yml and get an attestation, an immutable GitHub release and a PyPI upload with no second check. Fix: add a required reviewer to the release and pypi environments, put attest in the release environment so id-token is issued only after that gate, and limit ruleset bypass for refs/tags/v* creation to an explicit actor, not 'always' for the admin role.

The repository is now ClayGendron/wasi-python, so the next release's attestation will carry the new name and every user's documented gh attestation verify will fail, while the attest job's own check (release.yml:2484-2486, using $GITHUB_REPOSITORY) passes. hardening.note: Main-scope set caches are written by set-cache.yml's seed job (no in-run rebuild proof) and by release.yml's save-set on a main dispatch. actions/cache restore extracts with tar -P, so code running in any main-ref job (for example the Codecov uploader, fetched by version name at run time in the coverage job on a main dispatch) could plant an entry under a predictable key that later runs code in a branch reuse run's build job. hardening.note: context/research/2026-10-18-wasmtime-49-advisories.md:73 dismisses GHSA-hw8m-q44c-ggrf as 'no - GC proposal'. That reason is wrong: exnref is a GC-managed reference, wasm_gc and exceptions are both on in _engine, and the shipped module holds exnref locals live across 16562 try_calls. Until the floor is wasmtime>=49.0.2 (pyproject.toml:18 allows 49.0.0, the only 49.x on PyPI), a rebuild-time check that reruns this liveness scan (exnref locals live at try_table catch continuations must be zero) would keep the property from regressing quietly.

hardening.unit: The door host::call: guest pointers and lengths, admit before read, the answer buffer from
hardening.note: src/wasi_python/_call.py:1215-1223 _door_answer checks memoryview(response).nbytes, then calls bytes(response). For a bytes subclass with __bytes__, bytes() returns a different and larger object, so MAX_RESPONSE is not enforced on what is written. Observed: with MAX_RESPONSE patched to 1000, the guest received 5000 bytes (door_probe_output_run2.txt, bytes_subclass_over_max). A real answer of 2 GiB or more would also be truncated to i32 by wasmtime-py's Val.i32 when it is passed to host_alloc, while the bound check uses the full Python length. The effect stays inside guest memory, and only the trusted embedder's own host can cause it. Fix: convert first, then check, by doing data = bytes(response); if type(data) is not bytes: data = bytes(memoryview(data)); then if len(data) > MAX_RESPONSE: return None.

hardening.unit: The door host::call: guest pointers and lengths, admit before read, the answer buffer from
hardening.note: src/wasi_python/_call.py:1277-1281: when __bytes__ returns a bytes subclass, its __len__ runs on the guest thread, not on the home thread, and can disagree with the buffer that memory.write copies. Observed: the out length was 1 while 3000 bytes were written past a 1-byte allocation (len_lies). The effect stays inside guest memory, and only the embedder can cause it. The same fix closes it: always hand an exact bytes object to the guest thread.

hardening.unit: The 29 WASI calls the runner serves itself (mount linker) and the five it shadows (guard l
hardening.note: The trap path of the forwarded fd_readdir is left unzeroed. When a guest buffer crosses the end of memory, or `used` is out of bounds, wasmtime 49.0.0 writes whole entries (their padding from uninitialized host memory) and then traps. The guard runs only on errno 0, so nothing zeroes those entries. _shared then records the stop and returns EIO. The guest stops at its next function entry or loop header, so python.wasm cannot read the bytes. A hand-written wasm guest could read and fd_write them in straight-line code before that check: wasmtime's own fd_write is not shadowed and does not consult call.stopped. A crafted guest is outside the project's stated threat model, and the padding read zero on this host. Optional fix: zero [buf, buf+min(length, memory.size-buf)) in _fd_readdir when the forward raises, before re-raising.

hardening.note: _zeroed grows the stat trampoline's private page up to the guest memory's size. The store limiter's memory_size applies to each linear memory, so this second memory is bounded by memory_bytes on its own, not jointly with the guest's. Pages are reserved lazily and only the listing's bytes are touched, so resident growth equals the listing, which wasmtime already holds on the host. Joint accounting would make memory_bytes a whole-store bound.

But if the embedder's own wasmtime-py host function raises at the same time as a wasi_python guest traps, the runner's Func.__call__ paths (the run export, _initialize, host_alloc) can pick up that foreign exception and raise it from run(). This is upstream's design.

hardening.note: The Linux trap-handler check runs before each entry, not during a call. If a tool, host or provider replaces wasmtime's SIGSEGV or SIGILL handler during a call (for example with faulthandler.enable()), a guest trap later in that same call ends the process. The guest can choose when to trap, for example with an out-of-bounds read through numpy as_strided. Re-checking in the epoch callback or after each hand-off home would close the window.
